title: The race detector in the continuous integration pipeline

videos.script: go-concurrency lesson 16 taught the race detector at your desk. This lesson moves it into the pipeline, where nobody has to remember to run it. {{bug}} It starts with a race in hits. A parallel version of the counter, with a test that passes and a vet that says nothing. Run it six times and you get six different counts. Every one of them looks like a real number. One flag finds the bug, and names the line. {{blind}} Then what the detector cannot see. It watches one run of the program, and nothing else. A test with one worker never races. Neither does a machine with one CPU. Both pass, with the detector on. The cpu flag of go test fixes the second. {{cost}} Next, the price, measured on a benchmark. Several times the time, more than twice the memory, and one extra second at every exit. That price is why it runs in CI, and never in the binary you ship. {{pipeline}} Last, the pipeline itself. A workflow that runs every test with the detector, on every pull request. A race build for a staging run, with its reports going to a file. And one rule for a report: fix it. Never rerun the job until it goes green.
